Overall Structure of TRPM1
We first solubilized rTRPM1 in detergent glycol-diosgenin (GDN) under similar
EM
conditions as those used for the TRPM3 channel 33. However, the protein yield is poor (~80 µg
protein from 4 L HEK293 GnTI- cells) (Supplementary Fig. 2A), and subsequent cryo-EM
analyses failed to resolve the transmembrane domain (TMD) (Supplementary Fig. 3A). To
further stabilize the TMD, we incorporated 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-glycero-3-phosphocholine
(POPC), the most abundant lipid molecule on the plasma membrane, into the GDN micelles with
a detergent-to-lipid ratio of 10 to 1. The mixed micelle substantially improved the protein yield
by ~10-fold (Supplementary Fig. 2B). More importantly, the mixed micelle allowed us to
determine the structure of TRPM1 with an overall resolution of 3.6 Å with partial TMD density
resolved (Fig. 2A, Supplementary Fig. 3B and Supplementary Fig. 4). Using focused
classification and refinement, we improved the cryo-EM map of TRPM1 intracellular domain
(ICD) to 3.5 Å (Fig. 2B, Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. 5A). Despite the
minimal change in the absolute value of the resolution, the map quality of ICD was substantially
improved, especially in periphery regions (Fig. 2B).

The ICD of TRPM1 displays a 4-fold symmetrical structure with two layers of the TRPM
Homology Regions (MHRs) that are very similar to other TRPM channels (Fig. 2B) 54. This
observation contrasts with an earlier negative-stain EM structure showing a dimeric structure of
TRPM1 42.

We then mapped TRPM1 mutations that cause complete congenital stationary night
blindness (cCSNB) 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 onto our structure (Fig. 3). These mutations are distributed
evenly across the TRPM1 structure, with 10 mutation sites in the ICD and 1 in the TMD (Fig. 3).
Interestingly, the mutation in the TMD (F1120S) has been previously reported to inhibit proper
TRPM1 trafficking in native bipolar cells 14. Notably, Fig. 3 only displays the mutations within
regions visible in our cryo-EM map. As suggested by Fig. 3, most of the mutational sites in ICD
participate in maintaining the structural integrity of TRPM1, but their precise roles need to be
evaluated by functional assays in the future.

The Unique Architecture of the TRPM1 Transmembrane Domain
In our consensus map (Fig. 2A), only the voltage sensor-like domain (VSLD) is visible in
the TMD. To resolve the architecture of the entire TMD, we set out to improve the cryo-EM map
by three-dimensional (3D) classification. Our initial hypothesis was that the rotational
heterogeneity between TMD and ICD led to poor map quality. Therefore, we first aligned the
ICD by focused refinement, then classified inside the TMD without alignment. This strategy
indeed allowed us to resolve the cryo-EM density for the pore domain (PD), but at a much lower
intensity than the VSLD (Supplementary Fig. 6). This result suggests that heterogeneity
between the VSLD and PD within the TMD also contributed to the structural dynamics.
Therefore, instead of classifying the entire TMD, we first classified the PD, then classified the
VSLD among the particles that share a similar PND (Supplementary Fig. 4). This strategy
allowed us to determine the structure of the entire TRPM1 channel to an overall resolution of 4.3
Å using C1 symmetry (Fig. 4A and Supplementary Fig. 5B). Even though the local resolution
in the TMD is around 5-6 Å (Supplementary Fig. 5B), the cryo-EM map is unambiguous for the
transmembrane helices and the connections between them (Fig. 4A and Supplementary Fig. 7).
With this map, we attempted to build a model for the TMD of TRPM1 according to its sequence
and structural similarity with TRPM3 in the VSLD and the TRP helix (Supplementary Fig. 7
and Supplementary Tab. 1).

To our surprise, TRPM1 TMD displayed a unique arrangement in which the PD from one
TRPM1 protomer contacts the VSLD of the neighboring protomer in a clockwise orientation
when viewed from the extracellular space (Fig. 5A). A similar arrangement can also be observed
in our consensus map (Fig. 2A) when viewed with low contour levels. This TMD configuration
is opposite to that of TRPM3 33, 34, 35, the closest TRPM family member to TRPM1 (Fig. 4 and
Fig. 5A-C). This TMD configuration is also opposite to those from all published structures of
ion channels with similar architectures, including all TRP channels, voltage-gated potassium
channels, voltage-gated sodium channels, and voltage-gated calcium channels 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62,
63, 64. In other words, the TMD in TRPM1 is arranged with an inverted handedness compared to
all other related ion channels (Fig. 5A-C). Notably, the handedness here refers to the handedness
of the arrangement between VSLD and PD, not the handedness of the cryo-EM map. In fact, the
handedness of the VSLD region alone is conserved between TRPM1 and TRPM3 (Fig. 4A and
Fig. 4B).

Substantial alterations in the packing of TMD helices are necessary to achieve this inverted
configuration in TRPM1. Specifically, to reach the VSLD at the opposite side from the one in
TRPM3, the TRPM1 PD helices (S5 and S6) need to stretch out and extend at much shallower
angles with respect to the axis perpendicular to the membrane plane, resulting in a unique
curvature of S6 at its junction between the TRP helix (Fig. 4A). This possibly destabilizes S5
and S6 so that they adopt alternating conformations in neighboring protomers, making the TMD
of TRPM1 2-fold symmetrical (Fig. 5). Indeed, refinement imposing C2 symmetry yields a
better map (Supplementary Fig. 8). In one set of TRPM1 protomers, the S5 and S6 contact S1
and S4 at the extracellular side and run in parallel in the membrane (yellow and cyan in Fig. 5B
and 5C). In the other set of TRPM1 protomers, only S6 contacts S1 from the extracellular side,
while the S5 splays apart until forming close contact with S6 inside the membrane (blue and
salmon in Fig. 5B and 5C).

The Putative Ion Permeation Pathway in TRPM1
The unconventional organization of the TRPM1 TMD requires unique structural elements
to support the central ion permeation pathway. All ion channels with known structures use S6 to
form the pore. However, in rTRPM1 , S5 appears to line up the central cavity at the
EM
extracellular side (Fig. 5B, Fig. 5C, Fig. 6A and Fig. 6B). Nevertheless, at the intracellular side,
it is still S6 that forms the cavity comparable to the gate in other related channels (Fig. 5B, Fig.
5C, Fig. 6A and Fig. 6B). However, this observation does not automatically imply that the
equivalent gate residues in TRPM3 also regulate TRPM1 ion permeation. On the contrary, the
unique TMD in TRPM1 likely invokes the need for alternative gating mechanisms to control ion
permeation in TRPM1.

Globally, the inverted architecture in the TRPM1 TMD leads to an expansion of the central
cavity (Fig. 5A and Fig. 5B). Due to our limited resolution in the TMD, we cannot precisely
measure the diameter of the pore, but it is estimated to be at least ~10 Å, as the distance between
the Cα atom at the narrowest point (Y1013) is ~17.5 Å (Fig. 5D). We then compared the central
cavity between the narrowest point observed in rTRPM1 and the intracellular gate in other
EM
TRPM channels that were reported to be in the open or activated states (Fig. 5D). rTRPM1
EM
exhibited the second largest opening with a Cα-Cα distance from opposing protomers at ~17.5 Å,
about 1.5 Å narrower than the gate in the open-state TRPM2 65 (Fig. 5D). The Cα-Cα distance
between the other pair of opposing protomers in rTRPM1 is much larger due to the 2-fold
EM
symmetrical structure (Fig. 5D). On the contrary, the Cα-Cα distances at the intracellular gate in
open TRPM7 66, open TRPM5 31 and activated TRPM3 34 are 14.3 Å, 13.4 Å and 11.1 Å,
respectively. This observation is consistent with the hypothesis that TRPM1 itself is a
constitutively open ion channel 6, 8, 36, which is also supported by the results from our Ca2+
imaging experiments (Fig. 1B-D). However, we cannot rule out the possibility that some lipid
molecules can invade this pore in the cell membrane.

We then move on to test if the putative ion permeation pathway observed in our structure is
responsible for the TRPM1-dependent Ca2+ permeation observed in cells. To achieve this, we
chose the positively charged methanethiosulfonate (MTS) reagent, (2-
(trimethylammonium)ethyl) methanethiosulfonate bromide (MTSET), which is widely used in
ion channel research 67, 68, 69. The MTSET can readily conjugate to solvent-accessible cysteine
residues engineered at the channel pore and introduce a bulky side chain to prevent ion
permeation (Fig. 6C). We first confirmed that MTSET did not influence the Ca2+ permeation
ability of the wild-type (WT) rTRPM1 (Fig. 6D and Fig. 6E). We then introduced the Y1013C
EM
mutation on S5 inside the pore that is accessible from the extracellular side (Fig. 6A-C).
Notably, Y1013 forms the narrowest point in the putative pore in the rTRPM1 structure (Fig.
EM
5D). From similar Ca2+ imaging assays, this mutant was still able to permeate Ca2+ (Fig. 6D and
Fig. 6E), suggesting this cysteine mutation did not alter its function. However, MTSET
treatment substantially reduced the Ca2+ signals from this mutant (Fig. 6D and Fig. 6E).
This result suggests that the Y1013C on S5 likely directly contributes to constructing the pore.
This observation further supports the hypothesis that our cryo-EM structure of TRPM1 captures a
state that is close to its functional state in the HEK293 cell membrane.

Comparison of the ligand binding sites in TRPM3 and TRPM1
Despite the high sequence similarity in the S1-S6 helices between TRPM1 and TRPM3
(Fig. 4C), the inverted TMD architecture in TRPM1 makes it difficult to predict its
pharmacological properties entirely based on the sequence alignment. Therefore, in Fig. 7, we
compared both the sequence and the structure of the known ligand binding sites in TRPM3 and
their counterparts in TRPM1.

The VSLD of TRPM1 is structurally conserved with the VSLDs from all other TRP
channels (Fig. 4A and Fig. 4B). As a few TRPM3 ligands only interact with the VSLD, the
binding pockets for these ligands are preserved in TRPM1 (Fig. 7A and Fig. 7B). Additionally,
sequence alignment suggests that all key residues directly interacting with the ligands are also
conserved (Fig. 7A and Fig. 7B). These ligands include primidone (inhibitor) 34, 35, CIM-0216
(activator) 34, 35 (Fig. 7A), and phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP , obligatory) 33 (Fig.
2
7B). Therefore, our TRPM1 structure suggests that all these TRPM3 ligands potentially interact
with TRPM1.

We then tested if these ligands also regulated the function of TRPM1. We chose to focus on
primidone and CIM-0216, as our Ca2+ imaging assay required the reagents to cross the cell
membrane. Consistent with the structure comparison, pre-treatment with primidone substantially
reduced the Ca2+ signal (Fig. 7C and Fig. 7D, right panels), suggesting that primidone interacted
with and inhibited TRPM1. CIM-0216, however, did not significantly change the Ca2+ signal
(Fig. 7C and Fig. 7D, left panels). The observation can be simply explained by the assumption
that the majority of TRPM1 on the cell surface adopts a wide-open pore, as in our cryo-EM
structure, that cannot be further activated. It is also possible that some population of TRPM1 on
the cell surface adopts a non-conductive state unresolved by our cryo-EM analyses. However,
the predicted binding of CIM-0216 does not induce pore opening in this population of TRPM1,
possibly because its unique TMD configuration relies on alternative gating mechanisms.

Contrary to the VSLD ligands, pregnenolone sulfate (PregS) engages at a site between the
VSLD (S1) and PD (S6 and the pore loop) in the TRPM3 channel (Fig. 7E) 35. Due to the altered
helix packing in the TRPM1 TMD that is arranged with an inverted handedness, the PregS
binding site is no longer conserved in TRPM1 despite high sequence conservation in key binding
residues — PregS will sterically clash with S6 in both types of TMD-PD interface in the 2-fold
symmetrical TRPM1 (Fig. 7E). Indeed, PregS failed to increase the TRPM1-dependent Ca2+
influx in HEK293 cells (Fig. 7F and Fig. 7G). Nevertheless, this observation can also be
explained by the already wide-open pore in TRPM1 that may not be further activated by ligands.

[https://www.rcsb.org/structure/8ED7] into the cryo-EM map of TRPM1. The sequence was then
edited, and the coordinates were manually adjusted to fit the cryo-EM map using Coot v0.9.8 79.
Particularly, the TMD was modified by cutting out individual S5 and S6 helices in TRPM3 and
rotating them independently to fit the densities in the TRPM1 map. To facilitate model building
with an intermediate-resolution cryo-EM map, EMReady v1.2.1 80 was utilized to enhance map
quality, especially in regions exhibiting weak density. EMReady was able to substantially
improve the map in the ICD region, however, only minimal improvement was observed in the
TMD region. Therefore, we utilized the EMReady-enhanced map generated from C4 symmetry-
expanded particles to aid model-building in the ICD. On the other hand, to build the TMD
helices, we used the map refined in either C1 or C2, as the C4 symmetry is broken in the TMD.
Due to the limited resolution in the TMD, we used ISOLDE v1.7.1 81 to improve geometry and
model-to-map correlation. The models were then iteratively edited and refined in Coot v0.9.8,
ISOLDE v1.7.1 , and PHENIX v1.21.2-5419 82. The quality of the final models was evaluated by
MolProbity 83 in PHENIX v1.21.2-5419 . All figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX v1.7

Our initial intention was to keep the introduction on pharmacological regulation as simple as
possible as the results are largely controversial. In addition, most of the ligands, if not all, have not
been shown to act upon reconstituted TRPM1, making it difficult to distinguish if they directly
bind and gate TRPM1, or if they modulate TRPM1 via intermediate molecules in the retinal bipolar
cells. However, we do agree that it is better to include more information on this subject to
familiarize the readers with the field. Therefore, we added lines 56-69 in the introduction to expand
on previous findings related to pharmacological regulators.
We pre-incubated cells expressing TRPM1 with 100 μM voriconazole and did not observe a
significant decrease in the Ca2+ signal. We think voriconazole might be similar to capsaicin, which
is able to elicit a strong effect in retinal bipolar cells, but the effect might be related to some
intermediate components involved in TRPM1 gating. Consistent with this hypothesis, in Xiong et
al. 2015, voriconazole almost completely inhibited the TRPM1 current (~90%) elicited by
capsaicin, but only partially (~75%) inhibited the TRPM1 current elicited by mGluR6 antagonism.
We also acknowledge that voriconazole inhibits TRPM3 in a reconstituted setting (CHO and
HEK293 cells, Xiong et al. 2015), however, as the transmembrane domains of TRPM1 and
TRPM3 are very different, it is possible that the binding site for voriconazole on TRPM3 is no
longer conserved for TPRM1, or that the gating mechanism between TRPM1 and TRPM3 upon
voriconazole binding is different. Finally, we want to emphasize that even though we demonstrated
TRPM1 to work independently as an ion channel in this manuscript, we strongly believe that the
endogenous environment in the retinal bipolar cells, including the local lipid environment and
protein partners, are essential for reconstituting the native pharmacological properties of TRPM1.
As this result is not directly related to our central aim to report the first structure of TRPM1, we
decided not to include it in this manuscript. However, we plan to systematically characterize all
reported pharmacological regulators on TRPM1 using our Ca2+ imaging assay and report the
results in an independent manuscript that will be developed in the future.
We pre-incubated cells expressing TRPM1 with 50 μM primidone and observed a significant

based on our cryo-EM structures. This result also suggests that our Ca2+ imaging-based assay is
able to pick up inhibition, indicating the HEK293 cells may lack certain components to support
the voriconazole sensitivity of TRPM1.
